items.statement: A report from a routine internal quality audit that checks the quality system is working as intended may be discarded once all corrections arising from it have been verified.
items.quote: If the report in question was from a routine audit to verify that the firm's quality system is operating as intended, then it would be acceptable if the firm elected to discard the report once all corrections have been verified.
items.condition: routine audit report; after all corrections are verified

items.statement: Retain all documentation of corrective actions taken as a result of an internal audit.
items.quote: However, any documentation of corrective action as a result of such an audit would have to be retained (see §§ 211.180 and 211.188).

items.statement: When an internal audit finding leads to a process change, update all affected procedures, including the master production record, to reflect the change, and keep these records available for FDA inspection.
items.quote: For example, if a routine internal audit finds a problem with a mixing step and the outcome is a change in mixing time, all affected procedures, including the master production record, are to reflect the necessary changes, and such records are subject to FDA inspection as usual.
items.condition: when an audit finding leads to a process change

items.statement: Retain any investigation into the impact of an audit-identified problem on related batches and make it available for FDA inspection.
items.quote: Any investigation into the impact this problem had on related batches is to be retained and also made available for inspection by FDA (see § 211.192).

items.statement: Treat reports of investigations or evaluations prepared for matters such as product complaints, vendor qualification, periodic review of records and data, and failure investigations as records open to FDA inspection (not as internal audits), and retain them for at least the retention period set by the CGMP regulations.
items.quote: any reports of investigations or evaluations prepared in response to, for example, a product complaint (§ 211.198), vendor qualification (§ 211.84), periodic review of records and data (§ 211.180(e)), and a failure investigation (§ 211.192) are not internal audits as discussed above. Such records are subject to FDA inspection and must be retained for at least the time specified in the CGMP regulations (see § 211.180).

items.statement: Containers, closures and packaging materials may be sampled for receipt examination in the warehouse, provided the warehouse environment is suitable for the purported quality characteristics of the material sampled, so that sampling does not contaminate the contents.
items.quote: Yes. Generally, we believe that sampling in a typical drug manufacturing facility warehouse would not represent a risk to the container or closure or affect the integrity of the sample results. But whether the act of collecting a sample in the warehouse violates the CGMP requirement that containers "be opened, sampled, and sealed in a manner designed to prevent contamination of their contents..." will depend on the purported quality characteristics of the material under sample and the warehouse environment.
items.condition: warehouse environment suits the material's purported quality

items.statement: Sample containers or closures that are claimed to be sterile or depyrogenated under conditions equivalent to their claimed quality; a warehouse environment is not sufficient for this.
items.quote: For containers or closures purporting to be sterile or depyrogenated, sampling should be under conditions equivalent to the purported quality of the material: a warehouse environment would not suffice (see 21 CFR 211.94 and 211.113(b)).
items.condition: containers or closures purporting to be sterile or depyrogenated

items.statement: Perform all sampling of containers, closures and packaging materials so as to limit exposure to the environment during and after sample removal, e.g. by wiping outside surfaces, limiting the time the original package is open, and properly resealing it.
items.quote: At a minimum, any sampling should be performed in a manner to limit exposure to the environment during and after the time samples are removed (i.e., wiping outside surfaces, limiting time that the original package is open, and properly resealing the original package).

items.statement: Have well-written procedures for sampling containers, closures and packaging materials, and follow them.
items.quote: Well-written and followed procedures

items.statement: A shipment of containers or closures may be released for use on the basis of the supplier's certificate of analysis plus a visual identification of the containers or closures.
items.quote: Note that the CGMP regulations at 21 CFR 211.84 permit a manufacturer to release for use a shipment of containers or closures based on the supplier's certificate of analysis and a visual identification of the containers or closures.

items.statement: Once the supplier's reliability has been established by validating its test results, the visual examination of containers or closures may be performed entirely in the warehouse.
items.quote: Once a supplier's reliability has been established by validation of their test results, a manufacturer could perform the visual examination entirely in the warehouse.
items.condition: once supplier reliability is established by validating its test results

items.statement: Test representative samples of each shipment of each lot of every active and inactive component (raw material) to confirm its identity as labeled before releasing it for use in drug product manufacturing, using more than one test where needed to establish identity.
items.quote: These regulations require representative samples of each shipment of each lot of active and inactive component (or raw materials) to be tested to confirm the identity of the component as labeled prior to release for use in drug product manufacturing. The regulations acknowledge that more than one test may be needed to ascertain a component’s identity.

items.statement: In the sampling program for components, take samples that are representative of the shipment received.
items.quote: Samples are to be

items.statement: In the sampling program for components, base the number of containers sampled and the amount sampled from each container on statistical criteria for component variability, confidence levels and the degree of precision required.
items.quote: The number of containers

items.statement: In the sampling program for components, take into account the supplier's past quality history.
items.quote: The sample program

items.statement: In the sampling program for components, take a sample amount sufficient for the necessary analysis and for reserve samples.
items.quote: The sample amount

items.statement: Use an identity-testing approach for components that gives a high degree of confidence that each container in each shipment contains the material stated on its label.
items.quote: For these reasons, manufacturers need to develop an approach that provides a high degree of confidence that each container in each shipment contains the material purported by the label.

items.statement: Make all sampling representative and scientifically sound.
items.quote: (See also 21 CFR 211.160(b), which requires all sampling to be representative and scientifically sound.)

items.statement: Design the identity-testing approach to account for the fact that a material's identity must not vary from what is specified.
items.quote: The approach must account for the fact that the material’s identity must not vary from what is specified.

items.statement: Collect representative samples of each shipment of each lot of components for testing.
items.quote: The regulation at § 211.84 requires that representative samples of each shipment of each lot shall be collected for testing.

items.statement: Sampling and testing every container of a component for identity may be done, and may be particularly valuable for components bought from distributors.
items.quote: Testing samples from every container to determine identity may be valuable particularly for components purchased from distributors.

items.statement: The manufacturer may decide how many containers of a component to sample, as long as the sampling plan is scientifically sound, gives representative samples and follows the established principles for component sampling programs.
items.quote: The CGMP regulations permit each drug product manufacturer to make its own decision as to the number of containers to sample, as long as the sampling plan is scientifically sound, leads to representative samples, and complies with the principles established at § 211.84(b).
items.condition: plan scientifically sound, representative and in line with sampling principles

items.statement: Have the drug product manufacturer take component samples from the containers after receipt; pre-shipment or so-called piggyback samples are generally not acceptable.
items.quote: samples are to be taken by the drug product manufacturer from containers after receipt (i.e., pre-shipment samples or so-called piggyback samples are generally not acceptable)

items.statement: Do not composite samples taken from the top, middle and bottom of a single container when such stratified sampling is considered necessary (for example where moisture content needs to be controlled, especially when only part of a container may be used in a batch).
items.quote: Section 211.84(c)(4) explicitly prohibits compositing samples taken from the top, middle, and bottom of a single container when such stratified sampling is considered necessary (as might be the case when moisture content needs to be controlled, particularly when only a portion of a container may be used in a drug product batch).
items.condition: when stratified sampling is considered necessary

items.statement: Samples from a single container may be composited where compositing would not mask subdivisions of the sample that fail specifications.
items.quote: there "is no general prohibition... on compositing samples [from single containers] where such compositing would not mask subdivisions of the sample that do not meet specifications"
items.condition: where compositing would not mask failing subdivisions

items.statement: Testing individual samples from multiple containers is an acceptable approach that gives a high level of assurance.
items.quote: Testing individual samples from multiple containers provides a high level of assurance and is consistent with CGMP.

items.statement: A composite sample from multiple containers may be tested for identity only if the manufacturer demonstrates either that compositing does not mask detection of a single nonconforming container, or that additional test(s) routinely performed on the composite ensure that all sampled containers contain the same material.
items.quote: Testing a composite sample for identity could satisfy the CGMP regulations (§§ 211.84 and 211.160) but only if a manufacturer demonstrates either that the detection of a single nonconforming container is not masked by compositing or that an additional test(s) routinely performed on the composite sample ensures that all containers sampled contain the same material.
items.condition: only if masking is excluded or additional tests confirm sameness

items.statement: A purity assay on a composite sample made by mixing equal aliquots from each container may be acceptable, provided the test is sensitive enough to reveal a single nonconforming container.
items.quote: Thus, a purity assay on a composite sample prepared by mixing equal aliquots from each container may be acceptable provided such a test is sufficiently sensitive to reveal the presence of a single nonconforming container.
items.condition: provided the test detects a single nonconforming container

items.statement: Test at-risk components for melamine using a method shown to be suitable for detecting melamine adulteration, chosen on the basis of the manufacturer's risk assessment and prevention strategy.
items.quote: FDA recommends using a method demonstrated to be suitable for detecting melamine adulteration based on the manufacturer’s risk assessment and prevention strategy.

items.statement: When selecting the sampling approach and test method sensitivity for melamine, address the possibility that melamine is not uniformly distributed in an at-risk component, and that intentional contamination may originate in the starting material used to make that component.
items.quote: The manufacturer’s selection of a sampling approach and test method sensitivity should address the possibility that (1) melamine might not be uniformly distributed in an at-risk component, or (2) that the source of intentional melamine contamination might be the starting material used to produce the at-risk component.

items.statement: A less sensitive melamine method may be used for screening in certain cases.
items.quote: FDA also recognizes that a less sensitive method might also be appropriate for screening in certain cases.

items.statement: Control animal-derived ingredients so that contamination does not occur, from the initial collection and handling of the animal material through its processing and later use in the finished product.
items.quote: Yes, FDA requires that animal-derived ingredients be controlled in a manner to ensure that contamination does not occur, beginning with initial collection and handling of the animal-derived material through its processing and subsequent use in a finished pharmaceutical.

items.statement: As an ingredient manufacturer, take responsibility for the quality and safety of ingredients made for use in finished drugs, and manufacture them in conformance with current good manufacturing practice.
items.quote: Ingredient manufacturers are responsible for the quality and safety of the material they produce for use in finished pharmaceuticals. Ingredients are drugs and drugs are required to conform with current good manufacturing practice (FD&C Act, section 501(a)(2)(B)).

items.statement: As a finished drug manufacturer, take responsibility for the selection, qualification and use of ingredients in finished products.
items.quote: Finished pharmaceutical manufacturers are also responsible for their selection, qualification, and use of ingredients in finished pharmaceuticals (e.g., the CGMP regulations at 21 CFR part 211, subpart E).

items.statement: Fully understand the potential for pathogenic agent contamination of animal-derived ingredients, starting at the livestock processing establishment and continuing through later handling and processing, and establish stringent controls to prevent it.
items.quote: Ingredient and finished pharmaceutical manufacturers should fully understand the potential for pathogenic agent contamination beginning with the livestock processing establishment (LPE) and continuing through subsequent handling and processing, and establish stringent controls to prevent contamination.

items.statement: As part of the contamination control program for animal-derived ingredients, develop and apply appropriate tests or examinations to detect contamination.
items.quote: It is also essential that appropriate tests or examinations are developed and applied to detect contamination as part of any meaningful control program.

items.quote: One should assume that animal-derived materials will not only harbor but will often support growth of pathogens and accordingly should ensure appropriate control over the handling and processing of these materials.

items.statement: Follow CGMP when handling animal-derived material so that no contamination occurs that would affect its quality and purity or harm patients receiving the product.
items.quote: Current good manufacturing practice is to be followed in handling such material to ensure that contamination does not occur that would affect the material’s quality and purity, or that would be harmful when the product is administered to patients.
